title: Platform Operator Conversion Playbook — Integrations & Risk Reduction
author: Asha Patel
body:
Overview

This playbook is designed for platform and infrastructure engineers evaluating Redwood Inference for platform-wide adoption. It synthesizes positioning, concise messaging, competitive differentiators for technical buyers, a deployable pitch-deck outline, pricing scenarios tailored to platform teams, a sample conversion script for pilot-to-production, and a short anonymized case study focused on integration and risk reduction.

Use: Sales engineers, solution architects, and GTM leads should use this document during discovery calls, pilot proposals, and executive briefings.

1) One-line and three-line value props

One-line: Redwood Inference gives platform teams a predictable, cost-aware inference runtime that standardizes LLM serving across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments.

Three-line technical lead pitch:
- Unifies a single API and deployment model so your platform can standardize operators across teams.
- Optimizes for production economics with intelligent batching, KV/prefix caching, and deployment-aware routing to lower per-token costs without sacrificing latency SLOs.
- Ships with operational tooling (per-token traces, per-model dashboards, rollouts, and automatic fallbacks) to reduce incident surface area and migration risk.

2) Target audience and buyer personas

- Platform Engineer (primary): cares about standardization, SRE tooling, capacity planning, and predictable SLAs.
- ML Infrastructure Lead: cares about kernel selection, quantization profiles, and model lifecycle integration.
- Security/Compliance Engineer: cares about private control plane, KMS integrations, and audit logs.
- Product/Feature Owner: cares about unit economics, time-to-market, and quality regression protections.

3) Competitive brief (concise, technical)

Competitors considered: public LLM APIs, cloud-managed endpoints, and self-hosted inference runtimes.

- Public LLM APIs (ease vs control):
  - Strengths: fast time-to-value, simple API.
  - Weaknesses vs Redwood: opaque performance economics, limited private deployment options, and fewer operational controls for rollout and tracing.

- Cloud model endpoints / managed EC2-style services (scale vs ops):
  - Strengths: integration with cloud accounts, familiar billing.
  - Weaknesses vs Redwood: more custom glue required for batching/caching, inconsistent latency across model variants, and limited model-catalog performance tuning.

- Self-hosted inference runtimes (control vs maintenance):
  - Strengths: maximum control, potential lower cost at large scale.
  - Weaknesses vs Redwood: heavy ops burden, long iteration cycles for kernel/quantization tuning, and missing unified product/observability layer.

Redwood differentiators to emphasize to platform buyers:
- Single operational plane: standard API + rollout controls across hosted/dedicated/private reduces long-term platform fragmentation.
- Cost-aware controls: automated batching + prefix/KV cache policies with dashboard-level unit economics.
- Production tooling: token-level traces, per-model SLIs, canary rollouts, and automatic fallback to compatible model variants.
- Private deployment parity: same feature set and telemetry whether running hosted or on-prem.

4) Battlecard — objection/response quick hits

Objection: "We can self-host and save money."
Response: "At small-to-medium scale, self-hosted options incur hidden costs (engineering headcount, maintenance, kernel tuning). Redwood reduces total cost of ownership by combining runtime optimizations with a product surface for rollouts, tracing, and caching — accelerating time-to-value and reducing ops overhead. We provide transparent per-token reports so you can validate unit economics during pilot.

Objection: "We are concerned about data residency and compliance."
Response: "Redwood Private supports VPC and on-prem deployments with KMS/HSM integrations and audit logging. The private control plane mirrors the hosted feature set, so you do not trade observability for isolation.

Objection: "What if latency matters for small LLMs at high QPS?"
Response: "Redwood's runtime selects optimized kernels based on model shape and sequence distribution and offers dedicated GPU pools for predictable latency. We maintain latency SLOs and provide per-route latency breakdowns so you can tune batching vs SLO trade-offs.

5) Pitch deck outline (recommended 8 slides for technical buyer)

Slide 0: Title + Summarized Ask (pilot success criteria, target SLA, duration, sample QPS)
Slide 1: Problem statement for platform — fragmentation, cost unpredictability, and operational risk
Slide 2: Redwood solution overview — unified API + runtime + controls (diagram of hosted/dedicated/private parity)
Slide 3: Technical architecture (routing, batching, caching, KV store, model variants)
Slide 4: Operational story (dashboards, token-level traces, rollouts, SLI examples)
Slide 5: Pilot plan & success metrics (latency SLO, cost per 1M tokens, error rate, rollback criteria)
Slide 6: Pricing scenarios & sample math (see Pricing Scenarios section below)
Slide 7: Security & compliance checklist (network boundaries, KMS, auditability, certification status)
Slide 8: Next steps & integration asks (engineering contact, artifact list, timeline)

6) Pricing guidance + sample scenarios

Pricing considerations for platform decision-makers:
- Redwood pricing components: hosted token usage (generation + embedding), dedicated monthly reserved capacity (per GPU cluster), and private deployment license + support.
- Typical levers: batching configuration, sequence-length budgets, quantization profile, and cache hit rate.

Sample scenario A — Proof-of-Concept (3 months)
- Target: 250 RPS peak, 20 tokens avg per request, expect 20M tokens/month
- Offer: Hosted pilot with usage cap + 2-week committed dedicated capacity trial
- Estimated bill (hosted): 20M tokens * $0.0008/token = $16,000/month (example illustrative rates)
- Support: onboarding + 8h/week SRE engagement included in pilot package

Sample scenario B — Platform pilot to Dedicated migration
- Projection: 1B tokens/month at 30 tokens/request, 400 RPS peak
- Options: Reserved Dedicated cluster (monthly commit) vs continued hosted at volume discounts
- Break-even: Model savings from batching/quantization typically pay for a medium dedicated cluster at ~500M–800M tokens/month depending on model family and quantization.

Pricing nuance checklist to discuss during negotiations:
- Ask for your expected token mix (generation vs embedding) and sequence length distribution early.
- Validate cache-hit assumptions; a 20–40% prefix cache hit can materially reduce egress token costs.
- Discuss SLOs and required burst capacity. Dedicated clusters support burst policies to avoid overprovisioning.

7) Pilot-to-production conversion script (30-day cadence recommended)

Week 0: Kickoff & discovery
- Deliverables from prospect: sample workload traces, authentication plan, regulatory constraints, network topology diagram.
- Redwood deliverables: pilot environment, initial model catalog matching expected workloads, integration checklist.

Week 1: Integration & smoke tests
- Integrate auth (API keys or token exchange).
- Validate network connectivity for private/dedicated deployments.
- Smoke test with representative prompts and measure latency/throughput baselines.

Week 2: Tuning and observability setup
- Tune batching/windowing and prefix cache policies.
- Instrument token-level traces and SLI dashboards.
- Run quality checks vs golden prompt-sets to detect regressions.

Week 3: Load ramp & canary rollouts
- Gradually shift a small % of production traffic (5–10%) via canary.
- Monitor error budget, latency SLO, and cost per 1M tokens.

Week 4: Production cutover
- Execute full rollout or multi-stage expansion.
- Enable final redundancy/fallback policies and hand off runbooks to platform SRE.

8) Short anonymized case study — Acme Retail (platform integration)

Context: Acme Retail runs a centralized developer platform that exposes recommendation and search microservices. They needed unified inference across cloud regions and improved unit economics for recommendations.

Outcome highlights:
- Pilot: 6-week pilot focused on recommendations reranker and contextual embeddings.
- Cost: realized a 28% reduction in per-token spend after enabling prefix caching and optimized batching.
- Reliability: platform reduced inference-related incidents by 60% in the first 90 days due to canary rollouts and automatic fallback to smaller model variants.
- Time-to-value: integration took 2 engineers ~3 weeks to reach production canary.

Technical notes:
- Deployed Redwood Dedicated cluster in us-west-2, with private control plane for audit logging.
- Integrated KMS for model-encryption-at-rest and forwarded token-level traces into Acme’s centralized observability stack (Datadog).

9) Security FAQ for prospects (short, technical)

Q: Can Redwood run inside our VPC?
A: Yes. Redwood Private supports a customer-managed control plane that runs in your VPC or on-prem. Network egress is under your control, and private peering is supported for dedicated clusters.

Q: How is customer data encrypted?
A: Data is encrypted in transit (TLS 1.2+) and at rest. For Private deployments we integrate with your KMS/HSM for root keys. Access to logs and traces is role-based and can be shipped to your SIEM.

Q: Do you store prompt transcripts?
A: By default hosted telemetry stores anonymized traces for operational debugging. For customers requiring no telemetry persistence, Redwood offers telemetry exclusion options in Private deployments and controlled log retention policies.

Q: What compliance evidence is available?
A: Redwood maintains SOC2 Type II evidence and provides configuration checklists for customers to complete audits in Private deployments. Specific evidence bundles are shared under NDA.

Q: How do rollbacks and fallbacks work?
A: Rollouts are canary-based with automatic fallback policies. If a canary crosses configured SLO thresholds (latency/error), traffic is redirected to the previous model variant or a lower-cost compatible variant. Rollbacks are logged and auditable.

10) Integration checklist (developer-ready artifacts)

- Network diagram with allowed ranges
- Auth model selected (API key, OIDC integration, mTLS)
- Sample workload traces (.json) with timestamps and token counts
- Golden prompt set for quality/regression testing
- Compliance requirements (retention windows, audit frequencies)
- Target SLOs and error budgets

11) Appendix — sample CLI/test commands

Curl generation example:
curl -X POST https://api.redwood.ai/v1/generate \
  -H \"Authorization: Bearer <API_KEY>\" \
  -H \"Content-Type: application/json\" \
  -d '{"model":"rwd-compact-34b", "input":"Summarize product feedback:", "max_tokens":64 }'

Simple SLI query (example Prometheus-like):
- request_latency_seconds_bucket{route=\"/v1/generate\",le=\"0.1\"}
